newsitem.title: NORWAY: No cuts expected in Norway election year budget.
newsitem.headline: No cuts expected in Norway election year budget.

text.p: Norway will present a revised 1997 budget on Tuesday, but no extra spending cuts are expected with the next general election just four months away.
Many details are already known thanks to Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, who has been so open about the budget that traditional newspaper leaks have hardly been necessary.
Stoltenberg said last week he would raise the gross domestic product (GDP) growth and investment forecast for 1997 as well as lower jobless forecasts.

Officials said the budget would review the oil-rich country's investment strategy for the State Petroleum Fund, present options for the crown's relationship with a single European currency and discuss state control of Norway's two biggest banks.

The revised budget is a scheduled update of the 1997 budget, which was adopted in December and projected a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns ($7.9 billion). Thanks to Norway's oil production, this is the third consecutive year that it will run a budget surplus.
But Norwegian Central Bank Governor Kjell Storvik last week renewed a call for a tighter fiscal budget.

"My understanding is that there will be no revision of the budget, but we still hold the opinion that we would like to see a tighter budget than that which was decided by parliament in December," he said.

The central bank is concerned with longer-term inflation and believes a tighter budget would keep price rises more firmly under control at a time of falling unemployment and high capacity utilisation in industry.
In April, Norwegian inflation fell 0.1 percent month on month and rose 2.6 percent year on year, according to Statistics Norway, a government agency.
Oystein Stephansen, head of economic research at S-E Banken in Oslo, said: "I don't think they will present a tighter budget with sharp cuts. We are entering the election campaign."
Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland's Labour minority government, which has lost support in recent opinion polls, faces elections in September.
Stoltenberg would not reveal how much he would upgrade forecasts for GDP and investment growth, but said he would cut the unemployment forecast to 4.25 percent from 4.5 percent.
The finance ministry originally forecast overall GDP growth this year at 3.1 percent. Mainland GDP, which excludes the offshore petroleum industry, was seen to grow 2.5 percent.

Norway, the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia, invests its annual budget surplus in low-risk foreign government bonds but may soon start pumping the petroleum wealth into the world's major stock exchanges.
Stoltenberg said in February his ministry was thinking about increasing the risk element in the petroleum fund portfolio now that there seems to be more than enough to spend.
The petroleum fund, which now holds about 50 billion crowns, could total 270 billion crowns by the end of the year 2000, depending on oil prices.

In March, Stoltenberg also said the May budget would discuss the effect the euro, due to be introduced in 1999, would have on Norway's economy. The crown could be linked in some way to the euro, he said.

Norway cannot join European economic and monetary union (EMU) because Norwegians rejected European Union membership in a referendum in 1994. There are no plans to hold another plebiscite at least for the next several years.

Jagland said last October the government could reduce its controlling stake in the country's top commercial banks Den Norske Bank ASA (DnB) ) and Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse ASA to below 50 percent.

Jagland said it was important to maintain national control of the top banks, taken over during a financial crisis in 1988-92, but the government might reduce its share to about 33 percent in the next legislature.
($ = 6.969 Norwegian Crowns)
